messages.subject: Example code for multilevel ordered categorical model does not work
parts:
Trying to implement the example code from RStan website on multilevel ordered categorical model. Encountered several bugs, but could not debug the one as shown below:

Error in function stan::prob::categorical_log(i): Number of categories is 0, but must be between (1, 4)Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Stan code modified based on this.
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/models/ARM/Ch.17/17.6_multilevel_ordered_categorical.stan

This is my R code
#--------------------------------------------------------------------------
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- sample(c(0:3), 100, replace = T)
family <- sample(1:10, 100, replace = T)
N = length(x)
n_cut = length(unique(y)) - 1
n_family = length(unique(family))

dataList <- c("x", "y", "family", "N", "n_family", "n_cut")
fit <- stan(file = "./adsp.stan", data = dataList, iter = 1e3, chains = 4)
print(fit)

This is my Stan code
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> n_cut;
  int<lower=0> n_family;

  int<lower=0, upper=n_family> family[N];
  int<lower=0, upper=n_cut> y[N];
  vector[N] x;
}
parameters {
  vector[n_cut] mu_c;
  real mu_log_sigma;

  vector<lower=0>[n_cut] sigma_c;
  real<lower=0> sigma_log_sigma;

  matrix<lower=0>[n_family,n_cut] C;
  vector<lower=0>[n_family] S;
}
model {
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[N,n_cut] Q;
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[N,n_cut+1] P;

  mu_c ~ normal(0, 1000);
  mu_log_sigma ~ normal(0, 100);

  for (i in 1:n_family) {
    C[i,1] ~ normal(mu_c[1], sigma_c[1]);
    C[i,2] ~ normal(mu_c[2], sigma_c[2]);
    C[i,3] ~ normal(mu_c[3], sigma_c[3]);
    S[i] ~ lognormal(mu_log_sigma, sigma_log_sigma);
  }

  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (i_cut in 1:n_cut)
      Q[i,i_cut] <- inv_logit((x[i] - C[family[i],i_cut])/S[family[i]]);

    P[i,1] <- 1 - Q[i,1];
    P[i,2] <- Q[i,1] - Q[i,2];
    P[i,3] <- Q[i,2] - Q[i,3];
    P[i,4] <- Q[i,3];
  }

  for (i in 1:N)
    y[i] ~ categorical(transpose(row(P,i)));
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Example code for multilevel ordered categorical model does not work
parts:
Does the code as written work and it's just the modifications
that are problematic?

Sorry for the confusing error message. Stan indexes from 1,
not from 0.

> y[i] ~ categorical(transpose(row(P,i)));

so that y[i] must be between 1 and the size of row(P,i) [i.e.,
the number of columns of P].

Also, you can write transpose(row(P,i)) as P[i]'. Even better
to reorganize the data structure so that P is an array of
vectors. There's a chapter on arrays vs. vectors/matrices
in the manual.

- Bob

Xulong,

I haven't looked over the model, but the error you have is easy to fix:

On Thu, Jul 31, 2014 at 4:45 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:
Do you mean the y value in a categorical model should go from 1, instead 0? I actually tried this by assigning y as this: y <- sample(1:4, 100, replacement = T). But Stan returned an error being: y should be between 1 to 3. In my case I have 4 levels. n_cut was set as 3. Q matrix has 3 columns, and P has 4 columns. I will be very surprising if Stan can only handle y with 3 levels.
You've defined y as:
int<lower=0, upper=n_cut> y[N];

You've just said n_cut is set to 3.

This will give y values between 1 and 4, inclusive: y <- sample(1:4, 100, replacement = T). Stan is validating the data and telling you that your data does not match your bounds. Either define n_cut to 4 or you can even change the upper bound to "upper=n_cut+1".


Daniel

parts:
Thanks for being persistent. I just went and looked at the code:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/models/ARM/Ch.17/17.6_multilevel_ordered_categorical.stan

It looks like a literal translation of the BUGS code in Andrew
and Jennifer's book, and is not at all how you'd want to implement
this model in Stan.

Here are things wrong with that model at a glance:

1. Stan has a built-in ordered logit distribution and you really want
to be using that.

2. If you have a variable with constrained support, as in T[1,100] in
this model, then the parameters need to be declared to have matching
support, or you'll have a hard time with inits and/or sampling.

3. If you have truncations and have the support defined properly, then
you never need to have a T[...] truncation with just constants.

4. Rather than doing transpose(row(P,i)), which involves lots of extra
copying, it's better to set up the data structure for P so that it is
an array of vectors. See the manual chapter (near the beginning) on
arrays vs. vectors.

Mitzi's taking a pass through the ARM models, and will probably get
around to fixing this one. Peter might have time to fix it before then.

In the interim, I'd suggest looking at section 5.6 of the Stan 2.4
manual, which has a simple example of how to do ordered logit in
Stan.

- Bob

It seems there is a bug in the section 5.6 code on ordered logistic model if I am not creating it. File attached is a simplified version of my code to show the issue. Messages like below tend to show 1 or several times in the total of 1000 sampling attempts

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::ordered_logistic(N4stan5agrad3varE): Cut points parameter is 16.8437:0, but must be greater than 16.8437:0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

A separate question that I would like to confirm with you. Would a simple switch from the first line below to the second give me the exact lp__ samples that I can use to calculate the WAIC?
y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[n] * beta, c);
increment_log_prob(y[n], ordered_logistic_log(x[n] * beta, c));

Thanks,

Xulong

On Thursday, July 31, 2014 5:14:12 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Thanks for being persistent.  I just went and looked at the code:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/models/ARM/Ch.17/17.6_multilevel_ordered_categorical.stan

It looks like a literal translation of the BUGS code in Andrew
and Jennifer's book, and is not at all how you'd want to implement
this model in Stan.

Here are things wrong with that model at a glance:

1.  Stan has a built-in ordered logit distribution and you really want
to be using that.  

2.  If you have a variable with constrained support, as in T[1,100] in
this model, then the parameters need to be declared to have matching
support, or you'll have a hard time with inits and/or sampling.

3.  If you have truncations and have the support defined properly, then
you never need to have a T[...] truncation with just constants.  

4.  Rather than doing transpose(row(P,i)), which involves lots of extra
copying, it's better to set up the data structure for P so that it is
an array of vectors.  See the manual chapter (near the beginning) on
arrays vs. vectors.

Mitzi's taking a pass through the ARM models, and will probably get
around to fixing this one.  Peter might have time to fix it before then.

In the interim, I'd suggest looking at section 5.6 of the Stan 2.4
manual, which has a simple example of how to do ordered logit in
Stan.

- Bob

Thanks Bob for the valuable answer. I take it that the sampling process is still good and this message is okay to ignore. But, is there a way to get rid of messages like this? Given that this message always happen at the beginning of the sampling, it might be something to do with parameter initialization.

A separate question on the built-in ordered logistic model, ordered_logistic(). How does this function handles intercept? In the description of this model, part 33.6 in the Stan reference manual (page 297), can I write eta as alpha + beta * X with alpha the intercept? Alternatively, the intercepts are modeled in parameter c and eta can only include beta * X? I would like to put a mixed effect on the intercept specifically in my model.

parts:
No, there is no way to get rid of error messages like this.
There have been a gazillion mails on this list about them
and opinions vary, but they're staying in for now. (I've actually
been on the take-them-out side because I'm tired of responding
to all the mail we get about the message from new users. The
current compromise is that they are not going to say "error"
anywhere in them in the next round. If that doesn't work, we
may take more drastic measures in the future.)

The usual reason they occur is that discrete simulation of the Hamiltonian
needs to adapt its scales before it's numerically stable. So you can
get these warnings even if you initialize with a draw from the posterior.

Adding an intercept to an ordered logistic can lead to non-identifiability
depending on what the model is. For instance, if the cutpoints are
item-specific and the intercept is item-specific, you'll run into problems.
If one is fixed for each individual, then you still need to worry about
offsets, so you want to draw one with a prior with mean of 0.

- Bob

We have a built-in ordered categorical that might be more
convenient. We also have built-in ordered variables. There's
nothing in your model that makes sure the cuts C are
ordered, which will likely be a problem.

I couldn't follow what your S variable was doing. It looks
like you're using it to rescale differences, but that can easily
lead to multiplicative identities. Change c and correspondingly
change S and you get the same value.

Using normal(0,100) or normal(0,1000) is not good in Stan unless
you really expect the variates to be on those scales.

If the model works in Stan and produces a reasonably high
n_eff per iteration, then it should be OK.

Rather than

transpose(row(P,i)))

you can write

P[i]'

Oh, Bob! I think you were looking at my original model in my very first post, instead of the new one that I attached in my last post. All of the issues you mentioned have already been taken care of in this new one. Here I attach the file again. And also paste the code as below.

--- START ---

library(rstan)

rm(list = ls())

code <- '  // STAN: hierarchical ordered logistic model
data {
  int<lower=0> N;  // number of objects
  int<lower=1> K;  // number of categories
  int<lower=1> L;  // number of groups
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];  // response
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] sex;  // predictor
  vector<lower=1>[N] age;  // predictor
  int<lower=1,upper=L> group[N];  // group level predictor
}
parameters {
  vector[L] alpha;  // intercept
  real muAlpha;  // mu for intercept
  real<lower=0> sigmaAlpha;  // sigma for intercept
  real beta1;  // slope for sex
  real beta2;  // slope for age
  ordered[K-1] c;  // cutpoints for ordered logistic model
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] y_hat;
for (i in 1:N)

y_hat[i] <- alpha[group[i]] + beta1 * sex[i] + beta2 * age[i];
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(y_hat[n], c);
//  y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[n] * beta, c);
//  increment_log_prob(ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c));
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  for (n in 1:N)
    log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], y_hat[n], c);
//  log_lik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, c);
}
'

N <- 100  # number of objects
K <- 4  # number of categories
L <- 10  # number of groups
y <- sample(1:K, N, replace = T)
group <- sample(1:L, N, replace = T)
sex <- sample(0:1, N, replace = T)
age <- sample(50:100, N, replace = T)

dataList <- c("N", "K", "L", "y", "group", "sex", "age")
model <- stan_model(model_code = code, model_name='ordered_logitistic', verbose=FALSE)
fit <- sampling(model, data = dataList, iter = 1000, chains = 4)

waic <- function(stanfit){
  loglik <- extract (stanfit, "log_lik")$log_lik
  n1 <- nrow(loglik)  # number of samples
  n2 <- ncol(loglik)  # number of data points
  vars <- colSums((loglik - matrix(colMeans(loglik), n1, n2, byrow = T))^2) / (n1 - 1)
  pwaic <- sum(vars)  # effective parameter number
  lpd <- sum(log(colMeans(exp(loglik))))  # log pointwise predictive density
  waic <- -2 * (lpd - pwaic)
  return(list(WAIC = waic, Pwaic = pwaic, LPD = lpd))
}

print(waic(fit))

---END---

We have a built-in ordered categorical that might be more
convenient.  We also have built-in ordered variables.  There's
nothing in your model that makes sure the cuts C are
ordered, which will likely be a problem.

I couldn't follow what your S variable was doing.  It looks
like you're using it to rescale differences, but that can easily
lead to multiplicative identities.  Change c and correspondingly
change S and you get the same value.

Using normal(0,100) or normal(0,1000) is not good in Stan unless
you really expect the variates to be on those scales.  

If the model works in Stan and produces a reasonably high
n_eff per iteration, then it should be OK.

Rather than

 transpose(row(P,i)))

you can write

  P[i]'

- Bob

Looks OK to me.

You don't need to store the y_hat, but you can.

Ordered logistic hasn't been extended to vectors yet, so
you can't speed that up.

The only thing I can see to try would be a non-centered
parameterization here:
> alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha); // intercept

That is, take

alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1);

and define as either a local variable or a transformed
parameter,

alpha <- muAlpha + sigmaAlpha * alpha_raw;

- Bob

On Oct 10, 2014, at 1:12 AM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.

A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
that's non-zero for members of that group. You can identify with
a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
are estimated relative to it.

> 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.

That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).

You may also need to give c a prior.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] (ARM) Example code for multilevel ordered categorical model does not work
parts:
If a categorial id is not appropriate as a regression predictor, you want to change the example code in this link: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.12/radon_group.stan

In this file, the county id is obviously categorial but defined as int and used as a regression predictor.

> 1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.

You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.

A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
that's non-zero for members of that group.  You can identify with
a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
are estimated relative to it.  

> 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.

That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).

You may also need to give c a prior.

- Bob

No.  Unless I’m misunderstanding something here, county id in this example is used as an indexing variable, _not_ as a regression predictor.  The model has b[county[i]].  If it had b*county[i], then county id would be a regression predictor.  b[county[i]] is just fine.
A

> 1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.

You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.

A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
that's non-zero for members of that group.  You can identify with
a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
are estimated relative to it.  

> 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.

That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).

You may also need to give c a prior.

- Bob

On Sunday, October 12, 2014 11:05:41 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
No.  Unless I’m misunderstanding something here, county id in this example is used as an indexing variable, _not_ as a regression predictor.  The model has b[county[i]].  If it had b*county[i], then county id would be a regression predictor.  b[county[i]] is just fine.
A

On Oct 10, 2014, at 11:20 PM, Xulong Wang <emai...@gmail.com> wrote:

If a categorial id is not appropriate as a regression predictor, you want to change the example code in this link: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/ARM/Ch.12/radon_group.stan

> 1, the group level predictor in my model is simply the group id, which I defined as int, but in fact this is only a factorial variable in likes of R which do not have meanings of larger or smaller. Not sure whether this is appropriate.

You definitely shouldn't use a categorical ID as a regression predictor.

A typical approach is to give each group its own predictor
that's non-zero for members of that group.  You can identify with
a prior, or by giving one group no predictor in which case others
are estimated relative to it.  

> 2, you might have noticed there is an intercept term alpha in my model which I modeled on the group id, not sure whether the built-in ordered-logistic model would handle this well in terms of the identifiability issue with c.

That should be fine if the group IDs are centered. You
can't give them a hierarchical location (i.e., mean).

You may also need to give c a prior.

- Bob
